title: Le, les and se: indirect object pronouns
topic: indirect object pronouns; le / les → se before lo, la
why: The lesson moves from direct object pronouns (lo, la) to the indirect pronouns le / les, then to double pronouns like me lo, se lo, with the rule "le lo → se lo" that trips up every learner. It opens the unit on pronouns and prepares the next lesson, where these pronouns attach to the infinitive, the gerund and the imperative.

{"lessons": ["

To whom? Indirect object pronouns

You already know the direct object pronouns lo, la, los, las (I see him = lo veo). The indirect object answers the question \"to whom?\": I give a book to Marta → I give her a book. English uses the same words for both (\"I see him,\" \"I give him a book\"), but Spanish doesn't: \"to him / to her\" is le and \"to them\" is les.

PersonDirect (whom? what?)Indirect (to whom?)
yomeme
tútete
éllole
ellalale
ustedlo, lale
nosotros, nosotrasnosnos
vosotros, vosotrasosos
elloslosles
ellaslasles
ustedeslos, lasles

Good news: you already know these pronouns! They're the ones you use with gustar: me gusta, le gusta, les gusta. \"It's pleasing to me, to him\": that's an indirect object.

The big trap: le = to him, to her

Only in the 3rd person does le differ from the direct pronoun. Le escribo means \"I write to him / to her\"; \"I write it\" (the letter) is la escribo. And le works for a man as well as a woman: le escribo a Pablo, le escribo a Marta. So don't translate \"her\" automatically: ask yourself \"her, or to her?\"

Where does it go?

Unlike English, the pronoun goes before the conjugated verb, and in the perfect tense before haber:

Le he regalado un libro.I've given him (or her) a book.
No les digo nada.I don't tell them anything.
¿Le traigo la cuenta?Shall I bring you the check? (usted)

With usted, le also means \"to you\": that's why the market vendor asks you ¿Le pongo algo más?

", "

The double: le escribo a mi madre

Here's a habit that surprises English speakers: Spanish likes to say the indirect object twice. You use the pronoun le or les and the noun introduced by a.

Le escribo un mensaje a mi madre.I'm writing a message to my mother. (word for word: \"I'm writing her a message to my mother\")
¿Les has dicho la verdad a tus padres?Have you told your parents the truth?

In English, that extra \"her\" would be a mistake; in Spanish, it's the most natural sentence. And in two cases, the double is required:

  • when a + person comes first: A mi hermana le regalo un libro (just like A Marta le gusta el cine);
  • with a mí, a ti, a él, a ella… used for emphasis or to make things clear: Le escribo a ella, no a él.

Verbs that take an indirect object

VerbExampleTranslation
darLe doy mi número a Lucía.I give Lucía my number.
decir¿Qué le dices?What do you say to him (or her)?
regalarLes regalo flores.I give them flowers (as a gift).
prestar, dejar¿Me dejas tu paraguas?Will you lend me your umbrella?
devolverTe devuelvo las llaves mañana.I'll give you back the keys tomorrow.
enviar, mandarOs mando las fotos.I'll send you (all) the photos.
contarLe cuento todo a mi abuela.I tell my grandmother everything.
explicar¿Nos explicas el ejercicio?Can you explain the exercise to us?
enseñarTe enseño mi piso.I'll show you my apartment.
pedirLe pido ayuda a Javier.I ask Javier for help.
preguntarLe pregunto la hora.I ask him (or her) the time.

Pedir or preguntar? Both mean \"to ask,\" but you pide for a thing (help, a coffee, a favor) and you pregunta for information (the time, the way). Both take le or les. And in Spain, dejar very often means \"to lend\": ¿Me dejas tu bici?

", "

Two pronouns: me lo, te la, se lo

When there are two pronouns, Spanish always puts the indirect one first, then the direct one, and both go before the verb:

¿El libro? Te lo presto.The book? I'll lend it to you.
¿Las fotos? Nos las envía Diego.The photos? Diego is sending them to us.

English says \"I'll lend it to you\"; Spanish says, word for word, \"to-you it I lend.\" With me, te, nos, os, just remember: indirect, then direct, always in that order.

The golden rule: le lo → se lo

Le and les can never come right before lo, la, los, las. They turn into se:

SentenceOne pronounTwo pronouns
Doy el libro a Pablo.Le doy el libro.Se lo doy.
Doy la llave a Marta.Le doy la llave.Se la doy.
Regalo los libros a mis primos.Les regalo los libros.Se los regalo.
Devuelvo las llaves a la vecina.Le devuelvo las llaves.Se las devuelvo.

Se never changes: it means to him, to her, to you (usted), to them. To be clear, add a él, a ella, a usted, a ellos:

Se lo explico a ella.I'll explain it to her.

A three-step method: 1) find the direct object (what?) and pick lo, la, los, las to match its gender and number; 2) find the indirect object (to whom?); 3) if it's le or les, replace it with se. This se has nothing to do with the one in reflexive verbs like levantarse.

—¿Quién te regaló el reloj? —Me lo regaló mi abuela.— Who gave you the watch? — My grandmother gave it to me.
